workspaces.name: URL Journey
workspaces.description: Follow one HTTPS request across DNS, routing, transport, TLS, HTTP, packets, failures, and recovery.

workspaces.name: Failure Story
workspaces.description: Fail the active route and watch convergence, recomputation, failover, and the causal chain unfold.

workspaces.name: Network Builder
workspaces.description: Author topology and configuration, run probes, troubleshoot faults, use the CLI, rewind canonical time, and explain why the network behaves as it does.

workspaces.name: Packet Microscope
workspaces.description: Peel Ethernet, IP, TCP, UDP, and ICMP fields down to exact bytes and checksums.

workspaces.name: TCP Theater
workspaces.description: Handshake, sequence space, loss, retransmission, congestion response, and teardown.

workspaces.name: DNS Theater
workspaces.description: Recursive resolution, cache behavior, TTLs, retries, and visible failure boundaries.

workspaces.name: TLS 1.3 Theater
workspaces.description: Handshake negotiation, key schedule, certificate boundary, and encrypted application data.

workspaces.name: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3
workspaces.description: Compare multiplexing, TCP head-of-line blocking, QUIC streams, and recovery behavior.

workspaces.name: AS Routing Theater
workspaces.description: Explore deterministic interdomain relationships, valley-free policy, path selection, and route leaks.

workspaces.name: Physical Internet Atlas
workspaces.description: See facilities and physical Internet context on the globe without turning geography into forwarding truth.

workspaces.name: Internet Evidence
workspaces.description: Inspect edge-observed and public-collector evidence with explicit vantage and provenance boundaries.

workspaces.name: Measured Network
workspaces.description: Inspect imported or loopback-bridged local diagnostics without confusing one host vantage with Internet truth.

workspaces.name: Capture Replay
workspaces.description: Open a local PCAP/PCAPNG, follow conversations and time, inspect exact bytes, and keep missing evidence explicit.

events.title: Stub asks for a recursive answer
events.summary: www.example.test A leaves the client with RD=1.
events.detail: The application-facing stub resolver asks its configured recursive resolver to finish the job. Recursion Desired is set on this client-to-resolver query.

events.title: Recursive cache misses
events.summary: No usable answer or delegation is cached for this teaching query.
events.detail: Because the recursive resolver cannot answer from cache, it starts iterative resolution. Upstream queries are not asking those servers to recurse on its behalf.

events.title: Recursive asks the root
events.detail: The recursive resolver begins at the root of the namespace. The root need not know the final A record; it only needs to direct the resolver toward the next zone cut.

events.title: Root refers the resolver to .test
events.summary: The answer is not here; the next authority is the test. TLD.
events.detail: This is a referral, not the final A answer. It tells the recursive resolver which nameserver is authoritative for the next delegation step.

events.title: Recursive follows the .test delegation
events.summary: The same www.example.test A question moves one level deeper.
events.detail: Iterative resolution repeats the original question at the next authority. The recursive resolver is walking referrals until it reaches the zone that owns the name.

events.title: .test refers to example.test
events.summary: The authoritative nameserver for example.test is the next stop.
events.detail: The TLD server narrows the search from the top-level domain to the delegated example.test zone.

events.title: Recursive reaches the authoritative zone
events.summary: Now the resolver asks the server that owns example.test.
events.detail: The delegation chain has reached the authoritative source for the queried name. This server can provide the final A record instead of another referral.

events.title: Authoritative answer returns
events.detail: The authoritative response supplies the final address record. The TTL gives downstream caches an upper bound on how long this data may be reused without asking again.

events.title: Recursive caches the answer
events.detail: Caching is what makes the next identical lookup radically shorter. The cached record ages; it is not permanent truth.

events.title: Recursive returns the completed answer
events.detail: The stub sees one completed recursive answer even though the recursive resolver performed several iterative exchanges upstream.

events.title: Miss path complete
events.summary: Four network exchanges produced one cached answer.
events.detail: The useful artifact of the miss is not only the returned A record; it is also the cached state that can collapse future lookups.

event.title: Client offers TLS 1.3 parameters
event.summary: SNI www.example.test, ALPN h2/http1.1, X25519 key share, and TLS 1.3 cipher suites leave in the clear.
event.detail: ClientHello begins the handshake transcript. In this full 1-RTT model there is no PSK or 0-RTT data. The key share contributes to the later ECDHE shared secret.

event.title: Server selects the cryptographic context
event.summary: TLS 1.3, X25519, and TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 are selected.
event.detail: ServerHello completes the visible key-exchange negotiation. Both peers now have the information required to derive the ECDHE-based Handshake Secret and handshake traffic secrets.

event.title: Handshake traffic secrets become available
event.summary: ECDHE feeds the Handshake Secret; transcript(ClientHello…ServerHello) contextualizes client/server handshake traffic secrets.
event.detail: HOPSCOTCH represents this symbolically. It does not fabricate secret bytes. These handshake traffic secrets protect the encrypted authentication flight that follows.

event.title: The handshake crosses the encryption boundary
event.summary: EncryptedExtensions is the first server handshake message protected with server handshake traffic keys.
event.detail: Extensions not needed to establish the cryptographic context move here. In this model the server confirms ALPN h2 inside the encrypted handshake flight.

event.title: Server sends its simulated certificate chain
event.summary: www.example.test leaf → HOPSCOTCH Test Intermediate → HOPSCOTCH Test Root.
event.detail: The certificate message is encrypted under the server handshake traffic secret in TLS 1.3. The chain here is deliberately simulated and not a real trust anchor.

fields.label: Root
fields.value: HOPSCOTCH Test Root · simulated trust anchor

event.title: Server proves possession of the certificate key
event.summary: A signature covers the TLS 1.3 CertificateVerify context and the handshake transcript.
event.detail: The client verifies this signature with the public key from the end-entity certificate. This binds the authenticated identity to the handshake transcript.

event.title: Client validates identity and chain
event.summary: Hostname www.example.test matches; simulated chain and CertificateVerify proof validate.
event.detail: This local step is a teaching abstraction for certificate/path/hostname verification. No public CA claim is made and the displayed chain is intentionally synthetic.

event.title: Server authenticates the handshake transcript
event.summary: Server Finished verifies the handshake state and completes the server authentication block.
event.detail: Finished is a MAC over the transcript using a key derived from the server handshake traffic secret. The client must verify it before trusting the completed server handshake.

event.title: Master and application traffic secrets are derived
event.summary: The transcript through server Finished feeds client/server application traffic secret 0.
event.detail: TLS 1.3 derives application traffic secrets from the Master Secret and the transcript through the server Finished. The client still has one handshake-authentication message left to send.

event.title: Client Finished completes mutual key confirmation
event.summary: The client Finished is still protected with client handshake traffic keys.
event.detail: The client authenticates its view of the handshake transcript. After both sides have exchanged and validated Finished, this curated handshake is complete.

event.title: HTTP/2 request is now opaque TLS Application Data
event.summary: The record layer uses client application traffic secret 0 derived key/IV material.
event.detail: The protocol theater intentionally stops exposing application plaintext on the wire. HOPSCOTCH can still label the semantic payload because this is a curated teaching trace, not passive decryption.

event.title: Server responds under application traffic keys
event.summary: Encrypted TLS records carry the HTTP/2 response in the opposite direction.
event.detail: Client and server maintain separate application traffic secrets and therefore separate write keys/IVs. The record contents remain encrypted on the wire.

event.title: Authenticated encrypted channel established
event.summary: TLS 1.3 negotiation, server authentication, Finished verification, and application-key transition are complete.
event.detail: This deterministic trace now provides a stable bridge from DNS resolution and TCP transport into HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 application behavior.

event.title: Two responses begin concurrently
event.summary: Both lanes serve /hero.jpg and /app.js at the same time.
event.detail: HTTP/2 multiplexes frames for both streams over one TCP connection. HTTP/3 maps each request/response pair to an independent QUIC stream.
event.h2Label: H2 streams 1 + 3 share one ordered TCP byte stream
event.h3Label: H3 request streams 0 + 4 are independent QUIC streams

event.title: Both resources make forward progress
event.summary: Initial data for both streams reaches the client in both lanes.
event.detail: Before loss, multiplexing looks superficially similar: two application streams interleave over one connection.
event.h2Label: TCP delivers bytes in order to HTTP/2
event.h3Label: QUIC delivers ordered bytes within each stream

event.title: The same logical Stream A data is lost
event.summary: A transport packet carrying /hero.jpg data disappears in each lane.
event.detail: The loss event is synchronized to isolate the transport difference. The comparison is curated; packetization details are chosen to expose head-of-line behavior clearly.
event.h2Label: TCP sequence hole opens in the connection byte stream
event.h3Label: QUIC Stream A offset range is missing

state.phaseLabel: THE SAME LOGICAL STREAM A DATA IS LOST

event.title: Later data arrives after the gap
event.summary: Packets carrying later bytes—including Stream B data—still reach the receiver.
event.detail: The network can deliver packets out of order. What matters is what the transport is allowed to release upward to the HTTP layer.
event.h2Label: Later TCP bytes are buffered behind the missing sequence range
event.h3Label: Stream B bytes can be delivered independently of Stream A ordering

state.phaseLabel: LATER DATA ARRIVES AFTER THE GAP

event.title: The lanes visibly diverge
event.summary: HTTP/2 stalls both responses; HTTP/3 keeps /app.js moving.
event.detail: TCP presents one ordered byte stream, so a sequence gap prevents later connection bytes from reaching HTTP/2. QUIC has no ordering relationship between bytes on different streams, so Stream B can progress while Stream A waits for repair.
event.h2Label: CONNECTION HOL · Stream A + Stream B blocked
event.h3Label: Stream A blocked · Stream B still progressing

event.title: QUIC loss still affects the connection
event.summary: HTTP/3 avoids cross-stream ordering blockage, not all consequences of packet loss.
event.detail: QUIC recovery and congestion control are connection-level mechanisms. The curated trace shows reduced sending pressure while preserving Stream B delivery independence.
event.h2Label: TCP loss recovery / congestion response active
event.h3Label: QUIC loss recovery active · Stream B remains deliverable

state.phaseLabel: QUIC LOSS STILL AFFECTS THE CONNECTION

event.title: TCP retransmits the missing connection bytes
event.summary: Repairing the TCP sequence hole finally lets HTTP/2 see the buffered later bytes.
event.detail: Once the missing range arrives, TCP can release the contiguous byte stream. HTTP/2 can then resume parsing frames from both logical streams.
event.h2Label: TCP retransmission repairs the connection byte stream
event.h3Label: Stream B has already moved ahead

state.phaseLabel: TCP RETRANSMITS THE MISSING CONNECTION BYTES

event.title: HTTP/2 releases both stalled streams
event.summary: /hero.jpg and /app.js jump forward together after TCP repair.
event.detail: This is transport head-of-line blocking beneath HTTP/2 multiplexing: independent HTTP streams were coupled by the ordered TCP substrate.
event.h3Label: No equivalent cross-stream release event was necessary

event.title: QUIC repairs Stream A
event.summary: /hero.jpg receives the missing stream range while /app.js is already near completion.
event.detail: QUIC retransmits stream data as needed, but the lost Stream A range does not impose ordering on Stream B. STREAM frame boundaries need not be preserved during retransmission.
event.h2Label: Both H2 streams are progressing again
event.h3Label: Only Stream A needed ordering repair

event.title: Both lanes complete
event.summary: The final payload bytes are the same; the delivery coupling under loss was not.
event.detail: This theater isolates transport head-of-line behavior. It does not claim HTTP/3 can never block: flow control, congestion control, or QPACK dependencies can still create delays. This curated trace avoids dynamic QPACK dependencies.
event.h3Label: HTTP/3 complete with independent stream progress

event.title: Client opens the connection
event.summary: SYN consumes one sequence number and proposes CLIENT ISN 1000.
event.detail: The client sends SYN with SEQ 1000. A successful peer acknowledges 1001 because SYN occupies one position in TCP sequence space.

event.title: Server answers with SYN / ACK
event.summary: SERVER ISN 7000 acknowledges the client SYN with ACK 1001.
event.detail: The server combines its own SYN with an acknowledgment of the client sequence space: SEQ 7000, ACK 1001.

event.title: Connection established
event.summary: ACK 7001 completes the three-way handshake.
event.detail: The final ACK confirms both initial sequence numbers. Application data can now begin at client SEQ 1001.

event.title: Segment 1 arrives in order
event.summary: SEQ 1001–2460 advances the receiver next-expected byte to 2461.
event.detail: One full 1460-byte MSS arrives. The receiver is now waiting for byte 2461.

event.title: Segment 2 is lost
event.summary: SEQ 2461–3920 disappears before the server receives it.
event.detail: This missing sequence range creates a hole. TCP can recover it without waiting for the retransmission timer if enough later data arrives to produce duplicate ACKs.

event.title: Segment 3 arrives out of order
event.summary: SEQ 3921–5380 arrives, but byte 2461 is still missing.
event.detail: The receiver can buffer this later range, but its cumulative acknowledgment cannot move past the missing byte.

event.title: Duplicate ACK 1
event.summary: The server repeats ACK 2461: that is still the first missing byte.
event.detail: A duplicate cumulative ACK is evidence that later data arrived while the expected sequence did not.

event.title: Segment 4 extends the out-of-order queue
event.summary: SEQ 5381–6840 arrives while the 2461 hole remains.
event.detail: The receiver still cannot advance its cumulative ACK, so another duplicate ACK follows.

event.title: Duplicate ACK 2
event.summary: ACK 2461 repeats again.
event.detail: Two duplicate ACKs strengthen the loss signal, but this curated Reno scenario waits for the third duplicate ACK before fast retransmit.

event.title: Segment 5 arrives behind the same hole
event.summary: SEQ 6841–8300 arrives out of order.
event.detail: The receiver now holds three contiguous later segments behind the missing SEQ 2461–3920 range.

event.title: Duplicate ACK 3 triggers fast retransmit
event.summary: The third ACK 2461 crosses the curated Reno fast-retransmit threshold.
event.detail: The sender infers one segment was probably lost while the path still delivers later packets. It can retransmit without waiting for the retransmission timeout.

event.title: Reno enters fast recovery
event.summary: ssthresh falls to 3 MSS; cwnd is temporarily inflated to 6 MSS.
event.detail: For this curated Reno model, the 6-MSS flight is halved to a 3-MSS slow-start threshold. During fast recovery, cwnd is represented as ssthresh + 3 duplicate ACKs = 6 MSS.

event.title: Fast retransmit repairs the hole
event.summary: SEQ 2461–3920 is sent again immediately.
event.detail: The retransmission carries the exact sequence range identified by the repeated ACK 2461 signal.

event.title: One ACK releases the buffered ranges
event.summary: ACK 8301 cumulatively covers segments 2 through 5.
event.detail: Once the missing bytes arrive, the receiver already has SEQ 3921–8300 buffered. Its cumulative ACK can jump directly from 2461 to 8301.

event.title: cwnd deflates to ssthresh
event.summary: Fast recovery ends at cwnd 3 MSS, ssthresh 3 MSS.
event.detail: The full cumulative ACK confirms recovery of the lost range. This curated Reno model exits fast recovery by deflating cwnd to the 3-MSS threshold.

event.title: Forward progress resumes
event.summary: SEQ 8301–9760 crosses the repaired connection.
event.detail: The sender continues from the cumulatively acknowledged sequence point instead of replaying data that the receiver already buffered.

event.title: ACK 9761 grows the window again
event.summary: Successful delivery raises the illustrated congestion window to 4 MSS.
event.detail: The scenario now shows additive recovery rather than snapping immediately back to the pre-loss window.

event.title: Client begins teardown
event.summary: FIN at SEQ 9761 consumes one final sequence number.
event.detail: TCP teardown also uses sequence space. The peer will acknowledge 9762.

event.title: Server acknowledges and closes its side
event.summary: ACK 9762 plus FIN at SERVER SEQ 7001.
event.detail: For the compact theater sequence, the server combines its acknowledgment with its own FIN.

event.title: Final ACK closes the theater sequence
event.summary: ACK 7002 confirms the server FIN.
event.detail: The modeled exchange is complete. Real TCP endpoint state can persist afterward, such as TIME_WAIT, but this theater focuses on the wire exchange itself.

payload.title: Primary path established
payload.summary: Application traffic is flowing through R1 on the lowest-cost route.
payload.detail: The edge router prefers CLIENT → EDGE → R1 → CORE → APP with total metric 22. R2 remains a valid but more expensive standby path.

payload.title: Primary link fails
payload.summary: The R1 ↔ CORE adjacency disappears and the forwarding path is broken.
payload.detail: Traffic can no longer traverse the installed primary route. The physical failure is immediate; control-plane convergence is not.

payload.title: R1 floods new link state
payload.summary: R1 advertises that the R1 ↔ CORE link is no longer reachable.
payload.detail: The topology change begins propagating through surviving adjacencies. Routers are learning about the failure, but forwarding has not recovered yet.

payload.title: Failure knowledge propagates
payload.summary: R2 and CORE now share the updated topology view.
payload.detail: The link-state database converges across the surviving path. Once the relevant routers have the same topology, shortest-path calculation can produce a replacement route.

payload.title: SPF selects the alternate path
payload.summary: The failed edge is removed from the graph and the standby route through R2 wins.
payload.detail: CLIENT → EDGE → R2 → CORE → APP is more expensive than the original route, but it is now the lowest-cost viable path.

payload.title: Forwarding moves to R2
payload.summary: New traffic leaves the edge router on the alternate next hop.
payload.detail: The forwarding plane installs the replacement route. The route exists again, but the application still has to absorb the disruption that occurred during convergence.

payload.title: Traffic recovers
payload.summary: The application flow is healthy again over the alternate route.
payload.detail: The failed R1 ↔ CORE link remains down. Recovery comes from routing around the failure, not from restoring the failed link.
